summary: Arrays are the bedrock — and the techniques you learn here (prefix sums, carry-forward, sliding windows, contribution) come back in every harder topic. The job isn't 'iterate over an array'; it's 'pre-compute the right summary once so every query / scan becomes O(1)'. Master the index arithmetic of prefix sums and the symmetric thinking of carry-forward, and 70% of array problems collapse to two passes.

thoughtProcess.title: 1. Can repeated range queries be turned into prefix-sum lookups?
thoughtProcess.body: If you'll ask 'sum / count from L to R' more than once, build a prefix array first. Each query then becomes prefix[R] - prefix[L-1] in O(1). Watch the L=0 corner — return prefix[R] directly to avoid prefix[-1].

thoughtProcess.title: 2. Does each index need to know something about both sides?
thoughtProcess.body: Carry-forward. Walk left-to-right keeping one running summary (max so far, count of 'A's, latest min position) and right-to-left keeping the symmetric one. At index i you now have both halves in O(1) — pair them in a single final pass.

thoughtProcess.title: 3. Is the window length fixed (or constrained)?
thoughtProcess.body: Sliding window. Compute the first window, then slide one step at a time: window += A[r] − A[l]. O(N) total, never recompute from scratch. Works for fixed-size sums, averages, and 'longest with property X' once you generalise to two pointers.

thoughtProcess.title: 4. Are you summing the same quantity across MANY subarrays?
thoughtProcess.body: Contribution technique. Don't enumerate subarrays — ask 'in how many subarrays does index i appear?' The answer is (i+1) * (N−i). Multiply each A[i] by that count and sum once: O(N) instead of O(N^3). Watch overflow — use long.

thoughtProcess.title: 5. Is the input a matrix? Mind the index order.
thoughtProcess.body: Matrices are arrays of arrays. Row-major traversal is i for rows, j for cols. Column sum / transpose / diagonal walks just swap the loop order or add/subtract i±j. For rotation, transpose then reverse each row (90° CW) — write it as two clean passes, not one tangled one.

thoughtProcess.title: 6. Will sums overflow int?
thoughtProcess.body: N up to 1e5 and A[i] up to 1e9 means a full sum is up to 1e14 — needs long. Promote the prefix array and the running sum to long. Cast one operand to long BEFORE the multiply, never after.

thoughtProcess.title: 7. Is it a 'sum equals K' / 'count subarrays with sum K' — not a fixed length?
thoughtProcess.body: Fixed-length problems slide a window; variable-length sum problems need either a prefix-sum + HashMap of counts (works with negatives) or a two-pointer window (only valid when all A[i] are non-negative, so the sum is monotonic as the window grows). Pick by asking 'can values be negative?' before reaching for two pointers.

thoughtProcess.title: 8. Does the answer only compare within a fixed window? Then drop the division.
thoughtProcess.body: Least-average / max-average over a fixed size B: never divide. avg = sum/B and B is constant, so the minimiser of the sum is the minimiser of the average — comparing longs avoids floating-point ties and precision bugs (Subarray with Least Average).

commonMistakes.title: prefix[start - 1] when start = 0
commonMistakes.why: The L=0 case has no element on the left to subtract — return prefix[end] directly. Forgetting this throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException or, worse, returns garbage if you wrap with modulo.

commonMistakes.title: Storing prefix sums in int when they overflow
commonMistakes.wrong: int[] prefix = new int[N]; prefix[i] = prefix[i-1] + A[i];
commonMistakes.right: long[] prefix = new long[N]; prefix[i] = prefix[i-1] + A[i];
commonMistakes.why: 1e5 elements at 1e9 each = 1e14, which is way past int range (~2.1e9). The bug looks like correct logic returning negative or random values.

commonMistakes.title: Recomputing the window from scratch
commonMistakes.why: The brute is O(N*K). The slide is O(N). On N=1e5, K=1e3 that's 1e8 vs 1e5 — TLE vs instant.

commonMistakes.title: Enumerating subarrays to sum a quantity
commonMistakes.why: The product (i+1)*(N-i) stays within int until about N ~= 92,700; beyond that it silently overflows. Cast A[i] (or the product) to long so large arrays don't wrap.

commonMistakes.title: Mutating A in place when the caller doesn't expect it
commonMistakes.wrong:
// Equilibrium index — using A as prefix array
for (int i = 1; i < N; i++) A[i] += A[i-1];
commonMistakes.why: Looks clever, but if the caller reuses A later (multi-test-case harness, follow-up query) the values are corrupted. Allocate a separate prefix array unless the problem literally asks for in-place.

commonMistakes.title: Two-pointer leader scan written L→R
commonMistakes.why: Right-to-left with a running max is O(N). The L→R nested scan is O(N^2). Most 'is i greater than everything on its right?' problems collapse the same way.

commonMistakes.title: Matrix rotation done with extra space
commonMistakes.why: In-place rotation is the interview expectation. Two clean passes (transpose, reverse rows) is easier to remember than one tangled index mapping.

commonMistakes.title: 'Closest min-max' tracked with only one running variable
commonMistakes.why: A single 'last' loses track of whether you've seen the OTHER target yet. Track the two latest positions independently and pair them every time either updates.

commonMistakes.title: Two-pointer window on an array containing negatives
commonMistakes.wrong: while (sum > target) sum -= A[l++];  // assumes growth is monotonic
commonMistakes.why: Two pointers rely on 'adding an element never decreases the sum'. A negative A[i] breaks monotonicity, so shrinking/growing skips valid windows. Only use the sliding two-pointer for sum targets when all values are non-negative.

commonMistakes.title: Reusing one N for a rectangular matrix
commonMistakes.wrong: for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) { ... }  // assumes A[0].length == A.length
commonMistakes.right: int rows = A.length, cols = A[0].length; // use both; guard rows==0
commonMistakes.why: Transpose and column-sum inputs can be rectangular (rows != cols). Reusing one N over-indexes or misses cells. In-place transpose/rotate is only valid on square matrices; a rectangular transpose must allocate a cols x rows result.

commonMistakes.title: Counting pairs / subarray counts in int
commonMistakes.why: For N=1e5 the number of pairs approaches (5e4)^2 = 2.5e9, past int's ~2.1e9. The combinatorial total overflows even though individual elements are tiny.

keyPatterns.name: 1-D Prefix Sum
keyPatterns.when: Repeated range-sum queries on a static array, equilibrium-index problems, in-place running totals.

keyPatterns.name: Carry-Forward (left/right summary)
keyPatterns.when: Each index needs information from both sides — max-so-far on the right, count-so-far on the left, latest position of element X, etc.
examples: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock I

keyPatterns.name: Fixed-Size Sliding Window
keyPatterns.when: Sum / average / count over every window of length K. Compute once, then slide.
examples: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K
Subarray with Given Sum and Length

keyPatterns.name: Contribution Technique
keyPatterns.when: Summing a quantity across every subarray. Flip the question: how many subarrays contain index i? Answer: (i+1) * (N-i).

keyPatterns.name: Pick-from-Both-Sides (rolling boundary)
keyPatterns.when: Choose B elements from either end of the array; maximise sum. Start with all from left, then swap one left for one right at a time.
examples: Maximum Score from Card Picks (LeetCode parallel)

keyPatterns.name: Matrix Row × Column Traversal
keyPatterns.when: Column sums, diagonal walks, transpose, rotation. Pick the right loop nesting so the inner index varies fastest along the axis you're accumulating on.

keyPatterns.name: Prefix Sum + HashMap (subarrays summing to K, with negatives)
keyPatterns.when: Count or find subarrays with an exact target sum when values may be negative — a plain sliding window is invalid because the running sum isn't monotonic.

edgeCases: Single-element array — every prefix-sum index becomes a corner case (L = R = 0).
L = 0 in a range-sum query: don't read prefix[-1], return prefix[R] directly.
All elements equal — equilibrium / leaders / closest min-max all degenerate but must still return a valid answer.
Negative values present (Equilibrium / Pick-from-both-sides): the running min / running max can be negative, so don't initialise with 0.
Overflow when N is 1e5 and A[i] is 1e9 — prefix sums exceed int range; use long.
B > N in pick-from-both-sides → sum the entire array (handle in a guard or by clamping).
B = 0 → max sum is 0; the slide loop must not run.
Matrix with one row or one column — transpose / rotation must still work; diagonal loops must not over-index.
Empty string for AG counting — return 0 without crashing.
All maxes / all mins identical (Closest MinMax) — answer is 1 (the two values coincide on any index).
HashMap prefix-sum count: seed the map with prefix 0 -> 1 before the loop, or you miss every subarray that starts at index 0.
Two-pointer sum window: guard l <= r — the shrink loop can make l pass r when one element already exceeds the target.
Anti-diagonals: N=1 gives 2N-1 = 1 single-cell diagonal; a phase-2 loop starting at i=1 must not run.
Rectangular matrix transpose: output dimensions are cols x rows, not rows x rows — a square-only in-place swap corrupts data.
Least/max average by fixed window: all-negative arrays are valid — initialise bestSum from the first real window, never 0.
